episode_title: Remembering Paulien Cornelisse, and MPs push back on taxing small savers
description: The Netherlands mourns writer and comedian Paulien Cornelisse, who was still on TV every night when she died at 50. In The Hague, MPs push back on taxing small savers. Also today: border checks end but the military police get wider powers, mortgage rates hit a high for the year, prosecutors get tougher on attacks against public workers, and a Van Gogh could set an auction record.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: The Netherlands has lost one of its sharpest, funniest voices. Writer and comedian Paulien Cornelisse has died at fifty, while she was still on TV every night. And in The Hague, MPs push back on a plan to tax small savers.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Plus, the border checks end, but the military police get new powers. And a Van Gogh that could break the record.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: It's Thursday, the first of October. I'm Maya.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: And I'm Sam. This is Dutch Daily Briefing.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: We begin with a loss a lot of people here are feeling this morning. The writer and comedian Paulien Cornelisse died on Wednesday in Amsterdam. She was fifty.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: She died of cancer, with her loved ones around her. She'd been diagnosed in 2024.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: If you're new here, you might not know her name. But you've probably seen her face.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Almost certainly. Every weeknight she was the one-person jury on De Slimste Mens, 'The Smartest Person', one of the most-watched quiz shows in the country.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: And she was on screen right up to the end.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: The episodes were recorded before the summer. She wore a hat or a cap in every one, because chemo had made her hair fall out, and she didn't want a wig.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: No wig, no fuss.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Her real fame, though, came from language. In 2009 she wrote a bestseller called 'Taal is zeg maar echt mijn ding'. That's 'Language is, like, totally my thing'.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: The title does the joke for you.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: It sold seven hundred thousand copies. She picked apart how Dutch people actually talk: filler words, office jargon, the things people say without meaning them. Honestly, a gift if you're learning Dutch. She also wrote absurd books about a confused guinea pig who works in an office.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: And she had a new theatre show on the way.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: 'Waar was ik gebleven', 'Where was I'. It was due to open at Amsterdam's DeLaMar theatre later this month. It's been cancelled, with refunds for ticket holders. And the broadcaster, KRO-NCRV, dropped Wednesday's De Slimste Mens after talking with her family. The remaining episodes move back a day.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Prime Minister Rob Jetten called her 'sharp, funny and incredibly kind'.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Her last column in de Volkskrant came out just a week ago. She was wondering about the word 'apegapen'. It's Dutch for being utterly exhausted.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Curious about words right to the end.

segments.title: Border checks end, wider spot checks begin

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Next, the border checks with Belgium and Germany, which ended yesterday. Sort of.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: These were the checks brought in by the former asylum minister, Marjolein Faber of Geert Wilders' PVV, back in December 2024. They were meant to last six months, and then they were extended again and again.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Quick context: most of Europe is in the Schengen area, where you normally cross borders with no passport check. Countries can bring checks back, but only temporarily.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: And who was doing the checking?

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: The Koninklijke Marechaussee, the Royal Military Police. They guard borders, airports and the royal family.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: So why stop now?

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: The cabinet calls it a policy choice, after complaints about traffic jams from border towns and businesses. And the results were modest: about six hundred people refused entry, and two hundred and seventy arrests for things like people smuggling. The national audit office found the checks didn't cut migration.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: But there's a twist.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: From today, the Marechaussee goes back to spot checks anywhere within twenty kilometres of the border, but with more room than before. They get more hours on the same road each month, and there's no longer a six-hour daily limit. And on a selected train, they can now check every passenger.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Every passenger?

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: On that train, yes. Same for a selected flight from another Schengen country. But they can only pick up to a quarter of the trains or flights on a route.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: So if you take the train to Antwerp or Cologne, keep your ID handy.

segments.title: MPs balk at taxing small savers

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: To The Hague now, and a fight over taxing your savings.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Yesterday we told you the cabinet wants to cut the tax-free return in box 3, the tax on savings and investments, to a thousand euros. That would pull around 850,000 more people into it. Now, on day one of the big annual budget debate, that plan has hit a wall.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: It has. JA21, ChristenUnie and the SGP are against it, and so is Pro, on principle. The SGP's Flach called it 'a fine on thrift'. D66, VVD and CDA have no majority in either house, so they need those votes. After a barrage of questions, they said they'd look at alternatives. But D66 says any alternative has to raise the same money, about 473 million euros, from taxing wealth.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Has anyone come up with one?

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Not yet.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: The bigger fight, though, may be over income tax.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Both income tax rates go up next year, and a bigger tax credit for workers only partly makes up for it. The Council of State, the government's top legal adviser, points out that of six billion euros in extra taxes in 2027, 5.8 billion falls on workers.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: And this from a cabinet that says work should pay.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: BBB's Vermeer called it 'taking two hundred euros, giving back a hundred and expecting you to be happy.' JA21 and Pro say they'll only back the cabinet if that increase is scaled back.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: And that education fallback we mentioned?

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: D66 waved it off as the work of an 'overzealous civil servant'. But the VVD confirmed it's the agreed fallback if the social security savings fall short.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: And savers could take another hit even sooner.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: The cabinet also wants to nearly halve the tax-free allowance on savings and investments in 2027, to about thirty-one thousand euros per person. It's not law yet. Both houses still have to approve it.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Heinen gives the cabinet's answer later today.

segments.title: Mortgage rates peak as agents face a register

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Staying with your wallet, mortgage rates have hit their highest level of the year.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: How high are we talking?

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: The average ten-year fixed rate with NHG, the government-backed mortgage guarantee, is now four and a half percent. In mid-September it was around 4.2.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: And the European Central Bank hasn't even moved.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: No, this is the capital markets, where banks raise the money they lend you. Worries about inflation, energy prices and geopolitical tension push those rates up, and the banks pass it on.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: And that matters a lot here.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Because Dutch rules tie how much you can borrow to the interest rate. A couple earning ninety thousand a year could borrow about 413,000 euros at three and a half percent. At four and a half, it's about 395,000.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: So prices should come down?

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Not for now. Demand still far outstrips supply. But Amsterdam is cooling. In the second quarter, prices here were up less than one percent on a year earlier, against over four percent nationally. ABN Amro expects the cooling to spread, with prices flat or dipping slightly for the rest of the year.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Then there are the people selling those homes: estate agents.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Housing Minister Boekholt-O'Sullivan is taking oversight away from the industry. Every agent will have to be on a government register to work, and in serious cases they can be struck off.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: What's in it for buyers?

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Agents will have to show you the bidding log, the record of every bid on a home. That matters here, because bids are blind and people often go well over the asking price.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Concrete proposals are due early next year.

segments.title: Tougher sentences for attacks on public workers

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Now, attacks on police, paramedics and others who serve the public.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: From today, the Public Prosecution Service, the OM, has a new guideline. Every case of violence against someone in a public role goes to court. These cases can't be settled with a fine or community service anymore.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: And 'public role' covers a lot of people: police, emergency workers, public transport staff, teachers, referees, judges, journalists, politicians. Prosecutors now have to ask for double the usual sentence, with prison as the starting point. Justice Minister David van Weel gave an example: a first-time offender tries to seriously assault an emergency worker. There's no weapon and no injury. In principle, that's three months in prison. If the victim were an ordinary member of the public, it would be eighty hours of community service.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Is it mandatory jail, then?

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: No. It's what prosecutors ask for by default. Judges still decide.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: This follows New Year's Eve, when police and firefighters were attacked and sometimes lured into ambushes. And on the same day, rail staff sounded the alarm.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: The rail union VVMC sent an urgent letter. NS, the national railway, has had more than five thousand reports of aggression against staff so far this year. That's nearly double the figure for all of 2023. Conductors were knocked unconscious at Rotterdam Blaak and Den Dolder.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: What does the union want?

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: More security staff on trains. It also wants senior conductors to get back the enforcement powers NS cut in 2022 to save money. NS says it shares the concerns, and it's giving all conductors body cameras.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: And on one regional line, Arriva has told staff to let threatening fare dodgers go, instead of waiting around twenty-five minutes for police.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: The union says that's exactly the wrong answer.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Here in Amsterdam, a trial treating crack addiction has suddenly been halted.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: The idea's a bit like methadone for heroin users. Heavy crack users get a controlled dose of dexamphetamine, normally an ADHD medicine, to curb cravings. The long-acting version took twelve years to develop, in a project that includes the city health service, the GGD.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: So what happened?

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: The national health inspectorate, the IGJ, stopped production of the medicine at a hospital it won't name. It says it's concerned about the quality, but it hasn't said what the problem is.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: And people had already started taking it.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: They had, and their treatment's been interrupted. Amsterdam's health alderman, Alexander Scholtes, can't say how many people are affected. He called it 'the only promising method' for heavily addicted people. The GGD estimates there are three to nine thousand crack users in the city, many of them homeless.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Scholtes and Mayor Femke Halsema asked Health Minister Sophie Hermans to step in. She says she understands their concerns, but the inspectorate is independent, and 'I have confidence in their judgment.'

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: The research team has until the end of the year to decide whether the study can go on.

segments.title: Standoff with Italy over asylum returns

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Back to migration now, and a standoff with Italy.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Quick background: under the EU's Dublin rules, the country where asylum seekers first enter the EU is usually responsible for them. For years, Italy has largely refused to take people back.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: In June, Bart van den Brink, the same minister who ended the border checks, signed a declaration in Rome. Italy would take back people who'd travelled through it to the Netherlands. How's that going?

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Not well. In the first three weeks of the new EU migration pact, Italy carried out none of the twelve transfer requests it got. And Dutch courts keep blocking transfers, because the minister hasn't shown that Italy has reception places ready.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: So now he's threatening to hold back money.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Under the pact, the Netherlands pays about eleven million euros this year to help Mediterranean countries like Italy. Van den Brink told MPs: 'If something doesn't work, we won't pay.' He'll raise it with other EU ministers.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Sam, how much would you pay for a Van Gogh painting of a tree?

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Depends on the tree.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Chestnut trees in blossom. Sotheby's expects about 180 million dollars when it goes under the hammer in New York in November. Maybe over two hundred million.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: That would smash the Van Gogh record of 117 million. He painted it in May 1890, just after arriving in Auvers-sur-Oise. He died there two months later.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: And where's it been?

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: An Argentine collector family has had it since 1975. It was last shown in public in 1964, at the Guggenheim. It's been out of sight for sixty years. Whoever buys it, I hope they share.

segments.title: Fabel Friet and the price of a queue

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Staying with eye-watering sums, Amsterdam's TikTok-famous chip shop, Fabel Friet, may be costing its neighbours a fortune.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: This is the one where Nine Streets residents took the city to court over the queues, right?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Now a TU Delft researcher has studied more than six thousand Amsterdam home sales. Homes within five hundred metres of the shop sold for almost five percent less. That's about forty-one thousand euros.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Forty-one thousand euros. Because of fries.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Maybe. The study doesn't pin down the cause. And it runs from 2015 to 2023, but the queues only started in 2022.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: So most of that data is from before the shop had even opened.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: The judge rules in a few weeks. Meanwhile, an opinion piece in Het Parool told the complainers they're 'warmly welcome in Purmerend', the commuter town north of Amsterdam.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: And if you'd rather queue for something other than fries, here's what's on in Amsterdam this weekend.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Ghibli fans, this one's for you. From Friday to Sunday, composer Joe Hisaishi conducts the Royal Concertgebouw Orchestra at the Ziggo Dome in Zuidoost, and he plays piano too.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Spirited Away, Ponyo, Howl's Moving Castle, with film clips on a big screen. It's the orchestra's first visit to the city's biggest concert hall. Check the date before you book, though, because one night of their run is Beethoven's Ninth.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Also lovely, just less Ponyo. On Saturday, the H'ART Museum in the Plantage opens Chez Matisse. It has more than eighty works, including his famous La Blouse roumaine. It runs until February, so no rush.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: From tonight through Saturday, the Afrovibes Festival brings dance, theatre, music and spoken word by artists from Africa and its diaspora to De Brakke Grond, the Flemish cultural centre in the city centre. This year's theme is land, ancestry and belonging. Over the weekend it also moves into the Bijlmer Parktheater and Framer Framed, though the Bijlmer dates may still change.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Now, on Saturday from four till nine, IJver on the NDSM Wharf in Noord is throwing an anniversary party. Entry's free, and there are a thousand free oysters and a thousand free bitterballen.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: A thousand bitterballen? I'm taking an early ferry.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Good call, because they're only there while supplies last. Beer and spritz are two-fifty, and there's a DJ.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: And on Sunday, wind down at the Sunday Market at Westergas, in Westerpark. There's street food, local makers and art, and you can finish with a walk in the park.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: That's it for today. Thanks for listening to Dutch Daily Briefing. I'm Maya.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: And I'm Sam. See you tomorrow.
